\paragraph{Hard filtering and the epoch confound.}
Detect \& Remove (discarding samples with $q > 0.5$) achieves PPL 17.290 at full training length (6{,}103 steps, seed\,42), apparently outperforming all reweighting methods by a wide margin.
However, filtering discards 40\% of tokens, so the model sees the surviving real data ${\sim}$2.4 times versus once for reweighting methods.
An epoch-matched control (training D\&R for 2{,}533 steps to equalize content epochs at ${\sim}$1.0) yields 3-seed mean PPL $17.657 \pm 0.006$, within 0.006 of adaptive $\bstar$ ($17.651 \pm 0.007$).
The entire 0.360 PPL advantage of full-length D\&R is attributable to multi-epoch exposure, not to filtering itself (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_match}).
At equal compute, adaptive reweighting matches D\&R while requiring no detection threshold and retaining all training data.
D\&R also demands threshold calibration: raw PPL traces a U-shaped curve across thresholds ($q{>}0.1$: 17.40, $q{>}0.3$: 17.25, $q{>}0.9$: 17.42; Appendix~\ref{app:hybrid}), but this curve conflates filtering quality with multi-epoch exposure; preliminary epoch-matched comparisons ($q{>}0.3$: 17.74 vs.\ $q{>}0.5$: 17.66) suggest the apparent sweet spot reflects an epoch-diversity tradeoff rather than an optimal quality threshold.

By construction, $w_i = (1{-}q_i)^b$ assigns higher weight to lower $q_i$.

Full derivation in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}.

\paragraph{Why minimum intervention works.}
Restraint in downweighting outperforms aggressiveness.
In the 38.2\% of batches where $\aeff$ determines $\bstar$, the selected exponent is 4.9$\times$ lower than the ESS-only upper bound (\S\ref{sec:regime}), preventing unnecessary suppression of borderline samples ($q \approx 0.4$--$0.6$); this rate is robust across contamination levels (33.4\% at $\rho{=}0.6$) and seeds (CV ${<}2\%$).
$\aeff$ correlates with the true batch-level real fraction at Pearson $r \approx 0.70$ with a conservative bias of $-0.03$ (Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_validation}).

\paragraph{Where the advantage manifests.}
The advantage appears entirely at evaluation (PPL 17.65 vs.\ 17.69); training loss curves overlap (${\sim}1.4\%$ difference), consistent with reshaping the effective distribution.
Downstream benchmarks show 4 of 5 tasks with small negative $\Delta$ ($p \approx 0.19$, Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}), possibly reflecting evaluation-set distribution matching rather than true quality differences.
The aggregate mean $\bstar \approx 1.4$ as a fixed exponent yields PPL no better than uniform (17.693 vs.\ 17.694), confirming that per-batch adaptation is essential.

\paragraph{Failure analysis: low contamination and generative detectors.}
At $\rho{=}0.2$, the method degrades by $+$0.046 PPL relative to uniform.
The detector's mean $q$-score at this level (0.393) indicates poor discrimination: many clean samples receive moderate $q$-scores, and $\aeff$-binding occurs in ${\sim}$60\% of batches, meaning the method actively reweights rather than defaulting to $\bstar{=}0$.
The combination of active intervention and unreliable signal causes the method to suppress useful training data, consistent with our detector signal findings.
The generative detector failures (GPT-2 PPL at AUC\,=\,0.91, $\Delta{=}{+}0.10$; N-gram PPL at AUC\,=\,0.73, $\Delta{=}{+}0.13$) share the same mechanism: both assign high $q$-scores to fluent, predictable human text rather than to synthetic text specifically.
AUC alone does not determine effectiveness; what matters is whether the detector's $q$-scores separate provenance (discriminative signal) rather than fluency (generative signal).
TF-IDF+LR (AUC\,=\,0.94, ECE\,=\,0.048) succeeds because its features target lexical provenance markers.

\paragraph{Soft vs.\ hard filtering.}
The 3-seed epoch-matched experiment (\S\ref{sec:main-results}) resolves the apparent D\&R advantage: at equal content epochs, D\&R ($17.657 \pm 0.006$) and adaptive $\bstar$ ($17.651 \pm 0.007$) are equivalent ($\Delta{=}0.006$).
D\&R's best full-length PPL (17.250 at $q{>}0.3$) requires ${\sim}$3.2$\times$ effective training compute and a calibrated threshold: the raw U-shaped curve is entirely a multi-epoch artifact, as epoch-matched comparisons show monotonically decreasing PPL that saturates near the adaptive level (Figure~\ref{fig:dr_dual_curve}).
Reweighting sidesteps this tradeoff: no threshold to calibrate, no data discarded, and the parity at equal epochs ($\Delta{=}0.006$) suggests soft provenance-based weighting substitutes for hard filtration without information loss.
A hybrid approach (hard removal at $q{>}0.95$ combined with adaptive reweighting on the remainder, PPL\,=\,17.514) further improves PPL, but hard removal at any threshold assigns $w{=}0$, conflicting with the minimum intervention philosophy.
Given that epoch-matched analysis shows soft weights already match hard filtering, the hybrid's advantage likely also stems from multi-epoch exposure on the filtered subset; we leave controlled hybrid evaluation to future work.

\paragraph{$\tau$ as a practical dial.}
$\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$ all outperform uniform (Table~\ref{tab:tau}); sensitivity is asymmetric (over-cleaning degrades sharply, under-cleaning is mild), and $\tau \in [0.7, 0.8]$ is robust across $\rho \in \{0.4, 0.6\}$ (Appendix~\ref{app:tau_rho}).
$\tau$ remains an empirical hyperparameter; its theoretical derivation from first principles is an open problem (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).

\paragraph{Deployment guidance.}
The method requires a discriminative detector with AUC ${\geq}$ 0.94 (our tested threshold for positive $\Delta$); $\tau{=}0.8$ and $\nmin{=}\lfloor B/2 \rfloor$ serve as defaults that transfer across tested contamination levels and batch sizes.
When a high-confidence detector is available, practitioners may consider the hybrid variant for further gains, with the caveat that its advantage may depend on multi-epoch exposure.
Pareto-smoothed importance sampling diagnostics~\citep{vehtari2024psis} could provide per-batch reliability estimates for the weight distribution; we leave this integration to future work.

\paragraph{Domain-Level Data Mixing.}
A parallel line of work optimizes data composition without targeting synthetic contamination.
DoReMi~\citep{xie2023doremi} learns mixture weights via Group DRO~\citep{sagawa2020dro} with a proxy model, DSIR~\citep{xie2023dsir} performs importance resampling with $n$-gram features, and \citet{ye2025mixing} discover predictable functional forms relating mixing ratios to performance.
AIOLI~\citep{chen2025aioli} unifies these into an online adaptive framework, while \citet{yang2026mixing} train an RL agent for domain-weight selection.
DataComp-LM~\citep{gadre2024datacomp} and OLMo~\citep{groeneveld2024olmo} provide standardized benchmarks and open infrastructure for data curation at scale.
Continued pretraining~\citep{gururangan2020dont} adapts models to specific domains, a setting where contamination-aware methods are directly applicable.
These domain-level approaches do not address instance-level contamination within a domain.

\paragraph{Instance-Level Data Selection and Reweighting.}
Deduplication at the corpus level~\citep{lee2022dedup} is a prerequisite; data-constrained regimes~\citep{muennighoff2024scaling} and data quality filtering~\citep{longpre2024pretrainers} further shape training distributions.
SemDeDup~\citep{abbas2023semdedup} deduplicates via embedding similarity, SoftDedup~\citep{he2024softdedup} downweights high-frequency samples via $n$-gram commonness, and QuRating~\citep{wettig2024qurating} selects high-quality instances via learned quality scores.
Curriculum learning~\citep{bengio2009curriculum} and focal loss~\citep{lin2017focal} upweight examples by difficulty, \citet{sow2025dynamic} derive sample weights from per-sample loss with convergence guarantees, LESS~\citep{xia2024less} selects influential data for instruction tuning, and \citet{kuo2024weighting} show that differentiated weighting of LLM-generated data improves downstream classification.
Our reweighting differs from all of these in being driven by \emph{provenance} (detector scores estimating human vs.\ synthetic origin) rather than loss, frequency, quality, or domain membership.
